Main.sentence: Earth science or geoscience includes all fields of ___E:natural science U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_science)___ related to the planet ___E:Earth U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth)___ .

This is a branch of science dealing with the physical, chemical, and biological complex constitutions and synergistic linkages of Earth's four spheres: the ___E:biosphere U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biosphere)___ , ___E:hydrosphere U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrosphere)___ / ___E:cryosphere U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryosphere)___ , ___E:atmosphere U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmosphere)___ , and ___E:geosphere U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geosphere)___ (or ___E:lithosphere U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lithosphere)___ ).
Earth science can be considered to be a branch of ___E:planetary science U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planetary_science)___ but with a much older history.
___E:Geology U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geology)___ is broadly the study of Earth's structure, substance, and processes.

Geology is largely the study of the ___E:lithosphere U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lithosphere)___ , or Earth's surface, including the ___E:crust U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth%27s_crust)___ and ___E:rocks U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_(geology))___ .

It includes the physical characteristics and processes that occur in the lithosphere as well as how they are affected by ___E:geothermal energy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geothermal_energy)___ .

It incorporates aspects of chemistry, physics, and biology as elements of geology interact. ___E:Historical geology U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historical_geology)___ is the application of geology to interpret ___E:Earth history U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Earth)___ and how it has changed over time.

___E:Geochemistry U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geochemistry)___ studies the chemical components and processes of the Earth. ___E:Geophysics U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geophysics)___ studies the physical properties of the Earth. ___E:Paleontology U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paleontology)___ studies fossilized biological material in the lithosphere. ___E:Planetary geology U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planetary_geology)___ studies geoscience as it pertains to extraterrestrial bodies. ___E:Geomorphology U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geomorphology)___ studies the origin of landscapes. ___E:Structural geology U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Structural_geology)___ studies the deformation of rocks to produce mountains and lowlands.

Resource geology studies how energy resources can be obtained from minerals. ___E:Environmental geology U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Environmental_geology)___ studies how pollution and contaminants affect soil and rock.  ___E:Mineralogy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mineralogy)___ is the study of minerals and includes the study of mineral formation, ___E:crystal structure U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crystal_structure)___ , hazards associated with minerals, and the physical and chemical properties of minerals.  ___E:Petrology U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petrology)___ is the study of rocks, including the formation and composition of rocks. ___E:Petrography U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petrography)___ is a branch of petrology that studies the typology and classification of rocks.

___E:Plate tectonics U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plate_tectonics)___ , ___E:mountain ranges U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountain_range)___ , ___E:volcanoes U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volcano)___ , and ___E:earthquakes U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earthquake)___ are ___E:geological U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geological)___ phenomena that can be explained in terms of physical and chemical processes in the Earth's crust.

Beneath the Earth's crust lies the ___E:mantle U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth%27s_mantle)___ which is heated by the ___E:radioactive decay U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radioactive_decay)___ of ___E:heavy elements U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heavy_elements)___ .

The mantle is not quite solid and consists of ___E:magma U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magma)___ which is in a state of semi-perpetual ___E:convection U:(https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/convection)___ .
This convection process causes the lithospheric plates to move, albeit slowly.
The resulting process is known as plate tectonics.

Areas of the crust where new crust is created are called divergent boundaries , those where it is brought back into the Earth are convergent boundaries and those where plates slide past each other, but no new lithospheric material is created or destroyed, are referred to as ___E:transform U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transform_fault)___ (or conservative) boundaries.    ___E:Earthquakes U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earthquakes)___ result from the movement of the lithospheric plates, and they often occur near convergent boundaries where parts of the crust are forced into the earth as part of subduction.
Plate tectonics might be thought of as the process by which the Earth is resurfaced.

As the result of ___E:seafloor spreading U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seafloor_spreading)___ , new crust and lithosphere is created by the flow of magma from the ___E:mantle U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mantle_(geology))___ to the near surface, through fissures, where it cools and solidifies.
Through ___E:subduction U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subduction)___ , oceanic crust and lithosphere vehemently returns to the convecting mantle.
Volcanoes result primarily from the melting of subducted crust material.

Crust material that is forced into the ___E:asthenosphere U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asthenosphere)___ melts, and some portion of the melted material becomes light enough to rise to the surface—giving birth to volcanoes.

Atmospheric science initially developed in the late-19th century as a means to forecast the weather through ___E:meteorology U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meteorology)___ , the study of weather. ___E:Atmospheric chemistry U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_chemistry)___ was developed in the 20th century to measure ___E:air pollution U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_pollution)___ and expanded in the 1970s in response to ___E:acid rain U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acid_rain)___ . ___E:Climatology U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climatology)___ studies the ___E:climate U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate)___ and ___E:climate change U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_change)___ .

The ___E:troposphere U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Troposphere)___ , ___E:stratosphere U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stratosphere)___ , ___E:mesosphere U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesosphere)___ , ___E:thermosphere U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thermosphere)___ , and ___E:exosphere U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exosphere)___ are the five layers which make up Earth's atmosphere. 75% of the mass in the atmosphere is located within the troposphere, the lowest layer.

In all, the atmosphere is made up of about 78.0% ___E:nitrogen U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen)___ , 20.9% ___E:oxygen U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen)___ , and 0.92% ___E:argon U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argon)___ , and small amounts of other gases including CO 2 and water vapor.
Water vapor and CO 2 cause the Earth's atmosphere to catch and hold the Sun's energy through the ___E:greenhouse effect U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenhouse_effect)___ .

This makes Earth's surface warm enough for liquid water and life. In addition to trapping heat, the atmosphere also protects living organisms by shielding the Earth's surface from ___E:cosmic rays U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_rays)___ .

The ___E:magnetic field U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth%27s_magnetic_field)___ —created by the internal motions of the core—produces the ___E:magnetosphere U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetosphere)___ which protects Earth's atmosphere from the ___E:solar wind U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_wind)___ .
As the Earth is ___E:4.5 billion U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_of_the_earth)___ years old,   it would have lost its atmosphere by now if there were no protective magnetosphere.

___E:Earth's magnetic field U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth%27s_magnetic_field)___ , also known as the geomagnetic field, is the ___E:magnetic field U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetic_field)___ that extends from ___E:Earth's interior U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Structure_of_Earth)___ out into space, where it interacts with the ___E:solar wind U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_wind)___ , a stream of ___E:charged particles U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charged_particle)___ emanating from the ___E:Sun U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun)___ .

The magnetic field is generated by ___E:electric currents U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_current)___ due to the motion of ___E:convection currents U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convection_current)___ of a mixture of molten ___E:iron U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron)___ and ___E:nickel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nickel)___ in ___E:Earth's outer core U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth%27s_outer_core)___ : these convection currents are caused by heat escaping from the core, a natural process called a ___E:geodynamo U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geodynamo)___ .
The magnitude of Earth's magnetic field at its surface ranges from 25 to 65 μT (0.25 to 0.65 G).

As an approximation, it is represented by a field of a ___E:magnetic dipole U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetic_dipole)___ currently tilted at an angle of about 11° with respect to ___E:Earth's rotational U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth%27s_rotation)___ axis, as if there were an enormous ___E:bar magnet U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bar_magnet)___ placed at that angle through the center of Earth.

The ___E:North geomagnetic pole U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_geomagnetic_pole)___ ( ___E:Ellesmere Island U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ellesmere_Island)___ , ___E:Nunavut U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nunavut)___ , Canada) actually represents the South pole of Earth's magnetic field, and conversely the ___E:South geomagnetic pole U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_geomagnetic_pole)___ corresponds to the north pole of Earth's magnetic field (because opposite magnetic poles attract and the north end of a magnet, like a compass needle, points toward Earth's South magnetic field.)
Hydrology is the study of the hydrosphere and the ___E:movement of water on Earth U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water_cycle)___ .
It emphasizes the study of how humans use and interact with freshwater supplies.
Study of water's movement is closely related to ___E:geomorphology U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geomorphology)___ and other branches of Earth science.
Applied hydrology involves engineering to maintain aquatic environments and distribute water supplies.

Subdisciplines of hydrology include ___E:oceanography U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oceanography)___ , ___E:hydrogeology U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogeology)___ , ___E:ecohydrology U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecohydrology)___ , and ___E:glaciology U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glaciology)___ .
Oceanography is the study of oceans.
Hydrogeology is the study of ___E:groundwater U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Groundwater)___ .
It includes the mapping of groundwater supplies and the analysis of groundwater contaminants.

Applied hydrogeology seeks to prevent contamination of groundwater and ___E:mineral springs U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mineral_spring)___ and make it available as ___E:drinking water U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drinking_water)___ .
The earliest exploitation of groundwater resources dates back to 3000 BC, and hydrogeology as a science was developed by hydrologists beginning in the 17th century.
Ecohydrology is the study of ecological systems in the ___E:hydrosphere U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrosphere)___ .
It can be divided into the physical study of aquatic ecosystems and the biological study of aquatic organisms.
Ecohydrology includes the effects that organisms and aquatic ecosystems have on one another as well as how these ecosystems are affected by humans.

Glaciology is the study of the cryosphere, including ___E:glaciers U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glacier)___ and coverage of the Earth by ice and snow. Concerns of glaciology include access to glacial freshwater, mitigation of glacial hazards, obtaining resources that exist beneath frozen land, and addressing the effects of climate change on the cryosphere.
Ecology is the study of the ___E:biosphere U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biosphere)___ .

This includes the study of nature and of how living things interact with the Earth and one another and the consequences of that. It considers how living things use resources such as ___E:oxygen U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen)___ , ___E:water U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water)___ , and ___E:nutrients U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nutrient)___ from the Earth to sustain themselves.
It also considers how humans and other living creatures cause changes to nature.
Physical geography is the study of ___E:Earth's systems U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth_system_science)___ and how they interact with one another as part of a single self-contained system.
It incorporates astronomy, mathematical geography, meteorology, climatology, geology, geomorphology, biology, biogeography, pedology, and soils geography.

Physical geography is distinct from ___E:human geography U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_geography)___ , which studies the human populations on Earth, though it does include human effects on the environment.
___E:Methodologies U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methodology)___ vary depending on the nature of the subjects being studied.
Studies typically fall into one of three categories: observational, experimental, or theoretical.
Earth scientists often conduct sophisticated computer analysis or visit an interesting location to study earth phenomena (e.g.
Antarctica or ___E:hot spot U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hotspot_(geology))___ island chains).

A foundational idea in Earth science is the notion of ___E:uniformitarianism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uniformitarianism)___ , which states that "ancient geologic features are interpreted by understanding active processes that are readily observed." In other words, any geologic processes at work in the present have operated in the same ways throughout geologic time. This enables those who study ___E:Earth history U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth_history)___ to apply knowledge of how the Earth's processes operate in the present to gain insight into how the planet has evolved and changed throughout long history.

In Earth science, it is common to conceptualize the Earth's surface as consisting of several distinct layers, often referred to as spheres: the ___E:lithosphere U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lithosphere)___ , the ___E:hydrosphere U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrosphere)___ , the ___E:atmosphere U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmosphere)___ , and the ___E:biosphere U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biosphere)___ , this concept of spheres is a useful tool for understanding the Earth's surface and its various processes  these correspond to ___E:rocks U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_(geology))___ , ___E:water U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water)___ , ___E:air U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air)___ and ___E:life U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life)___ .

Also included by some are the ___E:cryosphere U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryosphere)___ (corresponding to ___E:ice U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ice)___ ) as a distinct portion of the hydrosphere and the ___E:pedosphere U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pedosphere)___ (corresponding to ___E:soil U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soil)___ ) as an active and intermixed sphere.
The following ___E:fields of science U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Branches_of_science)___ are generally categorized within the Earth sciences:
